## RCA — Phase 1 complete (mechanism CONFIRMED at runtime, not by inspection)

### 1. Runtime confirmation of the fail-open (the `dynamic` claim)

Confirmed by execution, twice, against a real malformed `rebar.toml` (invalid TOML ->
`_config_sources._parse_toml` raises `ConfigError`). Not read off the source.

**(a) At the function.** Same tmp root, three configs, `config.reset_config_cache()` between:

| config state | `gate_enabled(...)` |
|---|---|
| readable, `require_completion_verification_for_close = true` | `True` |
| **unreadable** (`[verify` — malformed TOML) | `False` + one stderr warning |
| readable, `= false` | `False` |

`r_unreadable == r_off` -> `True`. Byte-identical return; nothing on the value distinguishes them.

**(b) At a real consumer — a gated operation genuinely proceeds.** Driving
`gates.close_plan_review_gate_check(...)` (the plan-review CLOSE gate) with a real repo root:

```
OPERATOR TURNED GATE OFF   -> ok=True verdict='disabled' reason='plan-review close gate is disabled'
CONFIG UNREADABLE (fault)  -> ok=True verdict='disabled' reason='plan-review close gate is disabled'
```

Identical payloads. The gate returns **`ok=True`** — the close proceeds — and the returned
verdict actively asserts the gate is *"disabled"*, which is false: nobody disabled it. The fault
is laundered into a policy choice in the very field a later reader would consult. This is exactly
`mechanical-coherent-wolverine`'s R3 blocker, reproduced.

### 2. Caller sweep (BOTH methods, per docs/code-navigation.md)

Semantic (Serena `find_referencing_symbols` on `gate_enabled`) and a plain string `grep` agree on
**exactly 3 production call sites**:

| site | gate |
|---|---|
| `_commands/close_precheck.py:559` (`_completion_precheck`) | completion-verification CLOSE gate (billable LLM) |
| `_commands/gates.py:100` (`close_plan_review_gate_check`) | plan-review CLOSE gate (local HMAC, no LLM) |
| `_commands/gates.py:155` (`_plan_review_gate_applies`) | plan-review START-WORK gate (claim + transition open->in_progress) |

The string grep additionally found what the semantic search cannot see and which constrains the
signature: **~15 test modules monkeypatch the symbol by name** with a plain bool
(`monkeypatch.setattr(_gates, "gate_enabled", lambda *a, **k: True)`), plus
`_config_schema.py:159`'s `# read-via:` marker and
`tests/scripts/test_check_config_reads_heldout.py`'s `("require_plan_review_for_close",
"gate_enabled")` pair. Any signature that stops being bool-compatible breaks all of them.

### 3. Defect origin (`caused_by`) — the fix site is NOT the cause site

`git blame -w -C -M -L 63,92` on `gate_enabled` names **`051b82836bf`** (2026-06-24, "codebase-health
audit remediation ... gate/timestamp consolidation"). **That is a CARRIER, not the origin** — the
module docstring says so itself ("that resolution + fail-open posture is identical between them ...
so it lives here, once"): it *extracted* already-identical logic out of `transition.py` and
`claim.py`. `47c5626f8b7` (RP-04 C3c) is a second carrier (config-seam relocation only).

Walking back through them with `git log --all -S "could not read rebar config" --reverse -- src/rebar`:

| commit | date | what it did |
|---|---|---|
| `aa5c5fb6a6` (fe78) | 06-16 | signature close gate — **fail-CLOSED**, explicitly: *"a present-but-unreadable config must never silently disable the gate"* |
| **`85a77b9cc8`** (epic c7c5 WS-4) | **06-18** | **completion close gate introduced — first fail-OPEN, and the first bare two-valued skip** |
| `2873a91648` (epic 5fd2) | 06-23 | plan-review gate copies the fail-open posture |
| `051b82836bf` | 06-24 | carrier: consolidates the two copies into `gate_enabled` |
| `a78ea15a38` (28f1) | 07-13 | **removes the signature gate entirely** |

**Attribution: `c7c5-12ea-ad68-4690` (`slab-drove-stack`) — "LLM completion-verification close gate
(signed, optional)".** By **scope-of-work**, not by introducing commit: this is an *omission*. WS-4
wrote the fail-open skip as a bare `return None` beside gate-off's `return None`, and no commit ever
"broke" the distinction — it was never made. Its reviewer could plausibly have caught it; that WS is
where the third state was born unnamed. `85a77b9cc8` predates the `rebar-ticket:` trailer convention,
so the ticket was recovered from its "WS-4 of epic c7c5" subject line. Close class: **`preexisting`**.

Recording the divergence from the mechanical default, per protocol: a whole-file blame majority would
name `051b82836bf`; I am deliberately not naming it, because it is a pure extraction of pre-existing
behaviour.

### 4. Second, DISTINCT finding — the fail-open rationale has been silently invalidated

`gate_enabled`'s docstring defends fail-OPEN with three legs. Leg 2 reads:

> "The **stronger signature gate fail-CLOSES independently**, and a missing attestation is itself
> the 'not validated' signal CI checks."

**That gate no longer exists.** `a78ea15a38` (2026-07-13, `28f1-0ef8-65a4-4943`
`soppy-petit-alleycat`, "Retire verify.require_signature_for_close and its dead close-gate code")
deleted `require_signature_for_close`, `_signature_gate`, and `resolve_signature_gate`. A grep of
`src/rebar/` for all three returns **zero hits**. `85a77b9cc8`'s own commit message had named that
gate as reason (2) for why fail-open was safe.

This is a textbook **unmet obligation**: `soppy-petit-alleycat` removed a compensating control that a
consumer explicitly depended on, and did not update the consumer that names it. The date test detects
it — the implicated lines (06-24) predate the transition (07-13), so they cannot have caused it.

It is *not* the defect this ticket fixes (the collapse predates it by a month), so it does not take
the `caused_by`. It is recorded here because it is the decisive input to the fail-open question below,
and the stale docstring claim is corrected in scope.

comments.body:
## Decision: keep fail-OPEN; fix the COLLAPSE. (AC2's fail-closed clause is contested — operator ruling requested.)

The ticket asks for two changes. They are separable, and the evidence splits them:

* **the collapse** (one bool for two states) — no authority anywhere defends it; fixing it is pure gain,
  zero blast radius. **Doing it.**
* **the posture** (fail-open -> fail-closed, AC2) — a policy change with a large, measured blast radius.
  **Not doing it in this change**, on the evidence below. AC2 left unticked; filed as a follow-up for an
  operator ruling rather than silently deviating.

### Why not fail-closed — measured, not assumed

**A fail-closed gate on an unreadable config is not a gate that protects you. It is a gate that cannot
run and blocks everyone.** Counterfactual experiment: unreadable `rebar.toml`, `gate_enabled` forced to
report the gate active, drive `close_plan_review_gate_check`:

```
ok=False  verdict='unavailable'  reason='could not verify the plan-review attestation locally'
=> close is BLOCKED
```

Note the verdict: **`unavailable`, not a real verdict.** The config being unreadable is precisely what
makes the attestation unreadable too — the gate never actually evaluates anything. Fail-closed here buys
zero additional enforcement and costs a hard block. That asymmetry is the whole argument.

**Quantified blast radius on a machine with one malformed `rebar.toml`,** across all 3 production call sites:

| surface | fail-closed consequence |
|---|---|
| `_plan_review_gate_applies` | `rebar claim` **and** `transition open -> in_progress` hard-fail for every task/story/epic — you cannot start any work |
| `close_plan_review_gate_check` | `transition -> closed` hard-fails for every task/story/epic — you cannot finish any work |
| `_completion_precheck` | same, **plus** it would fire the billable LLM completion-verifier whose own `llm.*` provider/model/budget config lives in the same unreadable file |

**The decisive asymmetry: all three keys default `False`** (`_config_schema.py`
`require_completion_verification_for_close` / `require_plan_review_for_close` /
`require_plan_review_for_claim`). These are opt-in, default-off gates, so fail-closed would newly and
totally block **repos that never enabled any gate at all**. One malformed TOML character would stop work
in projects that made no security choice whatsoever. That inverts the default for the majority in order
to protect a minority — and per the experiment above, it does not actually protect them.

**Direct in-repo precedent for refusing exactly this trade:** `cautious-defamatory-verdin`'s amended
acceptance criterion deliberately declined a fail-fast because it "would convert a 2.1-hour hang into a
HARD FAILURE of every attested gate run on any partial clone, CI included." Same shape, same answer.

### The honest counter-argument, and why it does not carry (yet)

The strongest case *for* fail-closed is the finding in the RCA above: leg 2 of `gate_enabled`'s own
three-part fail-open rationale — "the stronger signature gate fail-CLOSES independently" — is **factually
false today**, deleted by `soppy-petit-alleycat` (`28f1-0ef8-65a4-4943`). Fail-open was a reasoned trade
with a named compensating control, and that control is gone. That genuinely weakens the original argument
and deserves to be on the record.

But it does not carry, for two reasons:

1. **Leg 1 is untouched and decisive** — "an unreadable config must not auto-enable a (possibly billable)
   gate across every repo and ticket." The default-off asymmetry above is leg 1, and nothing has changed it.
2. **Leg 3 survives** — a skipped gate mints no attestation, and that absence is the CI-checked
   "not validated" signal (`AGENTS.md`: a project that must keep force from circumventing a gate
   "enforces it by checking for that certification in CI").

So the correct response to the deleted compensating control is to **correct the stale claim** (done in this
change) and re-open the posture as its own decision — not to flip it inside a bug fix whose actual subject
is the collapse.

### What ships instead — and why it is strictly enabling, not a compromise

Making the two states **distinguishable at the source** is the minimum viable fix, and it is what the
downstream consumer actually needs. `mechanical-coherent-wolverine` does not need the gate to *run* on an
unreadable config; it needs to *record* `gate_unreadable` as a value distinct from `gate_off`, precisely so
that a fault is not laundered into a policy choice. Distinguishability delivers that in full.

It also leaves fail-closed available to anyone who later wants it, **per caller**, with no second config
read to drift out of sync — which is exactly the property the ticket's Approach section asks for ("fix it
at the SOURCE ... a second config read in a second place is a copy that will drift").

### Shape (backward-compatible by construction)

```python
class GateState(enum.Enum):
    ENABLED = "enabled"; DISABLED = "disabled"; UNREADABLE = "unreadable"
    def __bool__(self) -> bool: return self is GateState.ENABLED
```

`gate_enabled` returns `GateState`. `__bool__` is load-bearing and deliberate: the caller sweep found
**~15 test modules that monkeypatch `gate_enabled` by name with a plain bool**, and all 3 production
callers use `if not gate_enabled(...)`. Bool-compatibility keeps every one of them working and keeps the
fail-open posture byte-identical, so this change carries **no behavioural risk** — the new information is
purely additive.

To prove the distinction actually reaches a caller (rather than being theoretically available),
`close_plan_review_gate_check` gains a **distinct `unreadable` verdict** — `ok` stays `True`, so the close
still proceeds, but the payload no longer *asserts* the false claim that the gate is `disabled`. This
follows the precedent already documented in this very file for the `disposition` verdict: *"A DISTINCT
verdict, never 'exempt': the audit trail must separate ..."*.

**Wolverine's enum is now producible**: `_completion_precheck` can distinguish its `gate_off` and
`gate_unreadable` values by reading the returned `GateState`, with no change to `gate_enabled`'s signature
and no second config read — which was R3's stated blocker.

## Addendum — the documented contract settles the posture question (and finds a second stale doc)

Two authoritative sources found after the decision comment. Both point the same way, and together
they close the fail-open/fail-closed argument on citations rather than on judgement.

### 1. Fail-OPEN is the DOCUMENTED contract — so AC2 would be a regression against it

`docs/plan-review-gate.md:948-949`, describing `verify.require_plan_review_for_claim`:

> Default **off** ⇒ `claim` keeps today's behavior exactly. **An unreadable config fails this
> opt-in gate *off* with a warning (it never auto-enables across a repo).**

That is current, live documentation of the exact behaviour AC2 asks to invert. Flipping to
fail-closed is therefore not "hardening a gate" — it is **breaking a documented contract**, which is
precisely the move that turns a bug fix into a regression. Combined with the measured blast radius
(every `claim` and every close hard-blocked, in repos that never enabled any gate), the posture half
of this ticket is best classified **`intended-behavior`**, not a defect. It should not change without
an explicit operator decision, which is why it is being handed back rather than implemented.

### 2. The COLLAPSE, by contrast, violates the project's own stated design rule for gate config

`_config_sources._pyproject_rebar_state` resolves gate config to a **three-valued**
`"has"` / `"absent"` / `"unreadable"`, and says why:

> "An unreadable pyproject is reported as such — **NOT silently skipped** — so a present-but-
> unparseable **gate config** can fail CLOSED rather than **leaking the security gate**."

So the project already decided that an unreadable *gate* config must be reported as its own state.
`gate_enabled` simply never followed that rule. That is the authoritative intended-behaviour citation
making the collapse a genuine **`defect`** — independent of the reporter's framing, and independent of
wolverine needing it.

**The two halves of this ticket therefore have different legitimacy verdicts, and that is the whole
finding:** the collapse is a defect against a cited in-repo design rule; the fail-open posture is
documented intended behaviour. Fixing the first and leaving the second is not a compromise — it is what
the citations require.

### 3. Second stale artifact from the same culprit — `docs/config.md`

`docs/config.md:41-43` still asserts:

> "The **verify gate stays fail-closed**: a present-but-unreadable `verify.*` config **requires a
> signature to close**; an absent config leaves the gate off."

There is no signature-on-close gate any more — `soppy-petit-alleycat` (`28f1-0ef8-65a4-4943`) retired
`require_signature_for_close` on 2026-07-13. This is the same unmet obligation as the stale docstring
in `gate_enabled`: the removal did not update the two places that documented the guarantee it deleted.
An operator reading `docs/config.md` today is told `verify.*` fails closed when in fact it fails open —
which is very likely how AC2 came to be written.

Corrected in scope alongside the docstring, since it is the same false claim about the same function.

## Phase 2 complete — Gerrit change 1975

### RED -> GREEN, with a held-out oracle and two mutation checks

`tests/unit/test_gate_state_tristate_f5c4.py` (4 tests). **Physically moved out of the tree** before
the fix subagent was launched; it never saw the file, the assertions, or the path — only a contract card.

**RED first, for the right reasons** (3 failed / 1 passed, pre-fix):
* `..._are_distinguishable` -> `AssertionError: assert False != False`
* `..._three_states_resolves_to_its_own_named_value` -> `states collapsed: {'on': True, 'off': False, 'unreadable': False}`
* `..._not_report_an_unreadable_config_as_a_deliberate_disable` -> `assert 'disabled' != 'disabled'`
* `..._truthiness_is_unchanged...` **passed pre-fix** — deliberate: it is the invariance guard proving
  the fail-OPEN posture and bool-compatibility are untouched, so it must be green on both sides.

**GREEN after**: 4 passed, against an oracle the fixer never saw.

**Mutation checks — the test has teeth.** Two defect-seeded mutations, each restored after:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| `return GateState.UNREADABLE` -> `return GateState.DISABLED` (re-introduces the exact root cause) | **3 of 4 back to RED** |
| `if state is GateState.UNREADABLE:` -> `if False:` (drops only the caller-level distinction) | **1 back to RED** — the caller test is independently load-bearing, not redundant |

**Refactoring litmus**: every assertion is on observable output — enum members, the returned dict's
`ok`/`verdict`, and `bool()`. No private name, intermediate variable, or source grep. Renaming the new
`_close_gate_skip_result` helper or any internal would not break it.

### The fix

`src/rebar/_commands/gates.py` (366 -> 443 LOC, cap 800):
* `GateState(Enum)` — `ENABLED`/`DISABLED`/`UNREADABLE`, with `__bool__` truthy **only** for `ENABLED`.
* `gate_enabled(...) -> GateState`. Same stderr warning, byte-for-byte.
* `_close_gate_skip_result(...)` — extracted skip branches; `close_plan_review_gate_check` answers a
  distinct `unreadable` verdict, `ok` still `True`.
* Stale rationale corrected (the deleted signature gate); `docs/config.md` likewise.

**Backward compatibility is the design, not an afterthought.** `__bool__` is why all 3 production call
sites keep `if not gate_enabled(...)` with identical semantics and why the ~15 bool-monkeypatching test
modules are untouched. `_close_gate_skip_result` types its parameter `object` for the same reason.

### Scope & safety

* **Caller sweep** (both methods, above): 3 production sites; **zero behavioural dependencies broken** —
  truthiness is preserved for all three, so none needed changing.
* **Restoration, not creation** — no new command, artifact, or mutating external call.
* **No new dependency** — `enum` is stdlib and already used across `src/rebar/`.
* **No test weakened** — the fixer touched no existing test; `git status` shows only `gates.py`,
  `docs/config.md`, and the new test file.

### Gates

`make lint` PASS (complexity ratchet **`active=49 new=0 increased=0 stale=0`**) · `make typecheck` PASS
(598 files) · **625 passed, 14 skipped, 0 failed** across every unit/interface/lifecycle suite
referencing `gate_enabled`, `close_plan_review_gate_check`, `plan_review_precheck`, or
`_completion_precheck` — which covers the CLI, MCP, and library surfaces.

### Replication — the original report is gone

The exact scripts that produced the Phase-1 evidence, re-run unchanged:

```
READABLE + ON  -> GateState.ENABLED      OPERATOR OFF -> verdict='disabled'
UNREADABLE     -> GateState.UNREADABLE   UNREADABLE   -> verdict='unreadable'
READABLE + OFF -> GateState.DISABLED     ... "could not be read, so the gate was skipped
DISTINGUISHABLE? True                        — it was not deliberately disabled"
```

### Siblings (Step 7, both axes)

* **Construct axis** — swept every `except ConfigError` site in `src/rebar/`. Two confirmed siblings, both
  lower severity (they fail in the SAFE direction, so no gate is silently disabled): `config.mcp_readonly()`
  and `config.mcp_gate()`. **Filed as `spongy-rich-lizard` (8408-54bb-a8a5-49a7)**, linked `discovered_from`.
  Excluded with reasons: `_pyproject_rebar_state` (already three-valued — the precedent),
  `rebar_id_audit.py:152` (explicitly fail-CLOSED), `_operation_config.shadow_enabled` (env kill-switch),
  `_engine_support/gates.py:152` (numeric threshold).
* **Parity axis** — rule: *"resolving an opt-in review-gate policy flag must report a config-read fault
  distinctly from a deliberate off."* Census: CLI (`_commands/claim.py:181`, `transition.py:346`,
  `transition_close.py:443/465`) / MCP (`_mcp_writes.claim_ticket`) / library (`_lib_writes`) / automated
  callers / dual-direction (claim gate AND close gate) — **all route through the one `gate_enabled` core;
  no surface resolves these keys independently.** Confirmed by grepping the three key names across `src/`
  and `scripts/`: the only readers are the three call sites. **No MISSING slot.**
  (`test_review_bot.py::test_adapter_forces_gate_enabled` is a string-grep false positive — it concerns
  `gate_dispatch`'s unrelated `request.enabled`.)

### Wolverine's enum is now PRODUCIBLE

`mechanical-coherent-wolverine` R3 blocker 1 is cleared. `_completion_precheck` can now emit
`gate_off` vs `gate_unreadable` by reading the returned `GateState` — no second config read, no further
change to `gate_enabled`'s signature, no new edit site it does not own. R3 blocker 3 (authoring the
`gate_unreadable` / `disposition` ACs) is unblocked: the tri-state's shape is settled.

### Acceptance-criteria status (description deliberately NOT edited)

| AC | status |
|---|---|
| 1 — three-valued result, no caller can conflate | **MET** |
| 2 — unreadable FAILS CLOSED | **NOT MET, contested.** Evidence in the decision + addendum comments; handed to an operator as `loveydovey-preoceanic-geese` (39f8-ae7c-f651-4333). The "surfaced rather than swallowed" half IS met. |
| 3 — held-out test, RED before GREEN | **MET** (plus two mutation checks) |
| 4 — every caller updated; none relying on bool truthiness | **MET in substance, deliberately NOT in letter.** All 3 callers are correct for all three states, but they stay truthiness-based on purpose: `is GateState.ENABLED` would break the ~15 test modules that monkeypatch this symbol with a plain bool. The distinction is delivered where it is consumed (`close_plan_review_gate_check`'s verdict) rather than by churning call sites. |
| 5 — readable-config behaviour unchanged, existing tests unmodified | **MET** — 625 passed, zero test files modified |

### Attribution

`caused_by` -> **`c7c5-12ea-ad68-4690` (`slab-drove-stack`)**, by scope-of-work (omission at birth), close
class **`preexisting`**. Reasoning and the carrier walk that rejected the blame default are in the RCA above.

comments.body:
## Patchset 2 — the LLM reviewer caught a real gap in my caller sweep

Change 1975 PS1 got `LLM-Review +1` with two advisory (non-blocking) findings. The first was
**correct and I was wrong**, so PS2 acts on it rather than waving it through as advisory.

### The finding

> (regression) `transition_close.py` branches on the verdict string `!= "disabled"` to decide
> whether to install the locked-write recheck closure; the new `unreadable` verdict is
> `!= "disabled"`, so an unreadable config now installs and runs `plan_review_recheck`…
> [`src/rebar/_commands/transition_close.py:452`]

Verified in code:

```python
plan_review_recheck = None                       # transition_close.py:419
...
if check.get("verdict") != "disabled":           # :452
    def plan_review_recheck(locked_state): ...   # :454
...
pre_status_check=plan_review_recheck,            # :493  -> txn.py:386-387, INSIDE the write lock
```

So PS1 **did** change behaviour on the unreadable path: the closure got installed and ran an
extra config read (and a duplicate stderr warning) inside the write lock. My commit message
asserted "no behaviour change". That claim was false, and I did not catch it because my caller
sweep enumerated callers of **`gate_enabled`** but never swept consumers of
**`close_plan_review_gate_check`'s verdict string** — a second-order dependency. Recording the
gap explicitly: a caller sweep has to follow the changed *output*, not just the changed *symbol*.

There is a worse second-order case than the wasted read: if the config becomes READABLE between
the pre-lock check and the in-lock recheck, `locked_check` can return `ok=False` and BLOCK a
close that would previously have proceeded.

### What PS2 does

Reverted the `close_plan_review_gate_check` verdict split. The change is now **source-only**:
`GateState` and `gate_enabled`'s return type, with every observable payload byte-identical to
`origin/main`. `close_plan_review_gate_check` deliberately keeps one `disabled` verdict for both
states, with an in-code comment saying why and pointing at the follow-up.

**Why revert rather than widen the condition to `not in ("disabled", "unreadable")`:** that edit
lands in `_commands/transition_close.py`, which another agent is actively working. Per the
coordination boundary I was given, I stop at that file rather than collide. Widening to a tuple
would also be the same fragility with one more element — the real fix is an explicit
"did the gate run?" predicate, which needs to own both edit sites at once.

Filed as **`guardable-starred-milksnake` (2091-6d70-02a7-4e48)**, P2, linked `discovered_from`,
file-impact scoped to `gates.py` + `transition_close.py`, and it carries both halves: split the
verdict AND replace the string proxy with the predicate. The reviewer's second finding (the
`unreadable` verdict is untested through the close path) is folded into its ACs, since that test
belongs with the behaviour.

### Re-verified after the revert

RED with the pre-fix source restored (3 failed / 1 passed — the fourth is the invariance guard,
green on both sides by design); GREEN after (4 passed); mutation (`UNREADABLE` -> `DISABLED`)
returns **3 of 4 to RED**. `make lint` PASS with the ratchet at `new=0 increased=0 stale=0`,
`make typecheck` PASS (598 files), and **625 passed / 14 skipped / 0 failed** across every suite
referencing the changed symbols.

The fourth test was rewritten to pin the new contract honestly: it asserts the close-gate payload
is IDENTICAL for both states (the deliberate deferral) while the SOURCE still tells them apart —
so if someone later splits the verdict without fixing `transition_close.py`, that test fails.

### On the `Verified -1` for PS1 — not a code failure

`pytest (macos-latest, py3.13)` was **canceled at 72%**, not failed:
`##[error]The operation was canceled` after ~18 minutes. Zero `F` characters in the progress
output and zero failure keywords in all 1,120 log lines; the per-test `--timeout=300` never
fired. All three Ubuntu jobs (3.11 / 3.12 / 3.13) passed, as did lint, typecheck, mutation,
optionality, golden-path, and the authorship gate. That is a runner/job-level cancellation, not
a signal about this change — and PS2 gets a fresh run regardless, so no `recheck` was requested.

## Session handoff — the change MERGED but the ticket is not closeable as-is

State at handoff: `in_progress`. **Gerrit 1975 merged as `c504977aef`** (verified: one commit on
`origin/main` carries this ticket's trailer). **No attestation of any kind** is recorded — neither
plan-review nor completion.

**Blocker: 0 of 5 ACs are ticked.** I am not ticking them; this session did not verify them.

**One AC deserves particular care** — *"Every existing `gate_enabled` caller is updated to handle
the third state explicitly"* — because it is a caller-sweep claim, and this session repeatedly
found caller sweeps to be the thing that was incomplete. Verify it with **both** instruments, not
one: Serena's `find_referencing_symbols` for the semantic reference set, **and** a plain `grep`
for the symbol name as a string, since the LSP cannot resolve `getattr`/`monkeypatch.setattr`
targets and returns an empty result rather than an error. An empty semantic result is not
evidence of absence.

**Relevant context from this session:** `steep-tired-whimbrel`'s subject — `gate_enabled` failing
OPEN and collapsing gate-off with config-unreadable — is the same fail-open family catalogued in
`sphinxian-agrarian-snake` (twelve instances). It is also cited as a live blocker in another open
ticket's design notes, where the enum being proposed "cannot be produced without changing that
function's signature." Whoever closes this should check whether the merged change actually

## Problem
`gate_enabled` (src/rebar/_commands/gates.py:79-87) returns a BARE BOOL that is `False` for TWO
materially different states:

  * the gate is genuinely turned off (a deliberate policy choice), and
  * the gate's configuration could not be READ (a fault).

Worse, the unreadable case **fails OPEN**. An unreadable or malformed config therefore silently
DISABLES the completion-verification gate, and every downstream reader — including
`_completion_precheck` — sees a state indistinguishable from an operator having turned the gate off
on purpose. A fault is laundered into a policy choice, and the gate stops protecting anything
without anyone being told.

This is a latent defect with standalone value: it is worth fixing whether or not any dependent work
is ever built.

## Approach
Return a TRI-STATE (gate on / gate off / gate config unreadable) instead of a bool, and fail CLOSED
on unreadable rather than open. Fix it at the SOURCE in `gate_enabled` rather than recomputing the
distinction at each call site — a second config read in a second place is a copy that will drift out
of sync with the first.

Update all callers to handle the third state explicitly rather than defaulting it into either
existing branch.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `gate_enabled` returns a three-valued result distinguishing enabled / disabled /
      config-unreadable; no caller can conflate the latter two.
- [ ] An unreadable or malformed gate config FAILS CLOSED (the gate is treated as active), and the
      condition is surfaced rather than swallowed.
- [ ] A held-out test seeds an unreadable config and asserts the gate does NOT silently disable —
      demonstrated RED before the fix, not merely green after.
- [ ] Every existing `gate_enabled` caller is updated to handle the third state explicitly; a grep
      for call sites shows none relying on bool truthiness.
- [ ] Existing gate on/off behaviour is unchanged for readable configs (existing tests pass unmodified).

## Provenance
Split out per operator decision 2026-08-19 from `mechanical-coherent-wolverine` (23b2-1a94), where
this surfaced as plan-review R3's first blocking finding: 'gate_enabled must distinguish gate-off
from config-unreadable, or the expectation must be computed somewhere that can see the difference.
Its current fail-open bool is the blocker.' It is filed separately because the defect stands on its
own, and because wolverine cannot author its `gate_unreadable` acceptance criteria until this
tri-state's shape is settled.

Coordinate with RP-06 (`uneducated-habitual-primate`, 'Unified effective-policy discovery for review
gates'): RP-06's effective-policy snapshot should CONSUME this tri-state, not produce its own. This
was deliberately NOT folded into RP-06 so that a small, independently-landable fix is not coupled to
a large program's schedule.
